opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I can only speak from my own experience and from what's visible from the outside, so take this as a personal impression rather than an authoritative comparison.

My feeling is that the difference is less about specific algorithms and more about philosophy and priorities. At the technical level, everyone is doing broadly similar things: large-scale RL, reward models, verifiable rewards for math and code, and lots of effort on data and environments. The ideas spread quickly in this field, so it's hard to say that one lab has a fundamentally secret method the other doesn't.

What differs is what each lab chooses to optimize for and how it frames the problem. OpenAI, at least as I perceive it, has been very bold about pushing reasoning through RL. The o-series made a strong bet that if you scale RL on long chains of thought, you get qualitatively new capabilities. It's a frontier-pushing style: find the direction with the biggest upside and scale it hard.

Anthropic, from my perspective, has always thought of post-training as being closely tied to the model's character and behavior, not just its raw capability. There's a lot of attention on how the model behaves as an agent, how it handles ambiguity, whether it's honest, whether it does what the user actually wants. And there's been a very practical focus on coding and agentic tasks, things like working in a real codebase over many steps. So RL there is often less about solving a hard math problem and more about doing a long, messy, realistic task reliably.

I'd also say both labs have converged a lot. Everyone now realizes that the environment and the reward are the real bottleneck. The RL algorithm itself matters, but what matters more is whether you can build tasks that are close to what people actually need, and rewards that can't easily be hacked. That's where a lot of the real taste and craft goes, and that's where I think the labs differ most, in judgment about which tasks are worth investing in, rather than in some fundamentally different technique.

So if I had to summarize: OpenAI feels more like "scale the capability frontier and see what emerges," and Anthropic feels more like "shape a model that is useful and trustworthy in real work." But that's a simplification, and both are really trying to do both.

r001.rationale: It says both labs use broadly similar technical approaches and that their differences are more about priorities than fundamentally different methods.

r002.rationale: It describes shared use of verifiable rewards for math and code, and says both labs see task environments and rewards as central bottlenecks.

r003.rationale: It says the labs’ approaches are broadly similar, but does not state that experience showed distinct implementations from different companies could each work.

fable-5.1.text:
I should say upfront that I'll be careful here, because I've been inside both places and a lot of what I know is not mine to share. But at the level of philosophy, I think the differences are real and they're interesting, and they come from the two companies answering a slightly different question.

The way I'd frame it: OpenAI's post-training culture grew out of a very strong belief in scale and in general recipes. The instinct is, find the simplest thing that works, make it a clean objective, and then pour compute and data into it until the curve bends. That's how you get something like the o-series — reasoning as an RL problem over verifiable outcomes, run at enormous scale. There's a kind of engineering optimism there: don't over-design the environment, don't hand-craft too much, trust that the model will discover the behavior if the reward is right and you train long enough. And honestly that instinct has been vindicated more often than people expected.

Anthropic, at least as I experience it, starts from a different place. The question is less "what's the general recipe" and more "what do we actually want this model to be, and how do we make sure that's what we got." So there's a lot more weight on the specification side — what the model's character is, what it should refuse, how it should behave when the reward is ambiguous or when nobody's watching. Constitutional AI is the obvious public example, but the deeper thing is that the evaluation and the training are much more entangled. People spend a lot of time asking whether a gain on a benchmark reflects something the model genuinely understands or something it learned to game. The RL work is still very serious, but it's shaped by this constant worry about reward hacking and about generalization you didn't intend.

If I try to compress it: one culture optimizes for the recipe, the other optimizes for the model. Those sound similar but they lead to different day-to-day decisions. Which environments you build, how much you trust an automatic grader, how much human judgment you keep in the loop, how you react when the model does something impressive but slightly off.

What's funny is that they're converging. The stuff I cared about before any of this — agents, tool use, long-horizon tasks like SWE-bench or τ-bench — forces both approaches into the same room. Once the task is "actually do the job," you can't separate capability from behavior anymore. A coding agent that's brilliant but takes shortcuts is useless. A careful agent that can't finish is also useless. So the OpenAI-style scaling instinct and the Anthropic-style "what did we actually build" instinct end up needing each other.

And I'd add one more thing, which is the point I keep making about the second half. The bottleneck is shifting from training methods to evaluation. Both labs have very good RL now. The gap is in asking the right questions — what environments, what tasks, what counts as success. That's where I think the real differentiation between labs is going to show up over the next few years, more than in the optimizer.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes distinct philosophies—OpenAI optimizes for a general recipe, while Anthropic focuses on the model’s specification—and says the approaches are converging. It does not characterize them as fundamentally similar.

r002.rationale: It describes OpenAI using RL with verifiable outcomes, but Anthropic’s approach is framed around specification, evaluation, and concern about ambiguous rewards. It does not identify seeking clear, objective feedback as a shared strategy.

r003.rationale: The response says OpenAI’s scaling instinct has been vindicated and that both labs now have very good RL, communicating that approaches at both companies can work.

astra-6.text:
我会把这个问题拆成两层：一层是希望模型学会什么，另一层是通过什么反馈让它学会。因为我们没有两家公司完整的内部信息，所以很难直接说，OpenAI 用的是一种强化学习方法，Anthropic 用的是另一种。

从思路上讲，后训练里其实有两类不太一样的问题。一类是，什么样的回答更符合人的偏好，比如更有帮助、更诚实，或者更注意安全。这里的难点在于，标准本身就不完全明确，而且不同目标之间可能有冲突。另一类是，模型能不能把一个任务做成。如果结果可以验证，强化学习就可以围绕成功与失败提供反馈。但即便如此，如何定义任务、如何设计奖励，也会影响模型最后学到什么。

所以我更愿意从目标、反馈和应用场景这几个维度去比较两家，而不是把它们概括成两条完全不同的技术路线。一个产品看起来更强调某种风格或能力，不一定说明它背后的强化学习算法有本质区别，也可能来自数据、奖励设计，或者产品层面的选择。

对我来说，真正值得关注的是：后训练到底是在让模型更会表达它已经知道的东西，还是让它获得了完成更复杂任务的能力？要判断两家的差异，最终还是要看具体任务上的行为和结果，不能只看它们怎么描述自己的方法。

r001.rationale: The response cautions against assuming the companies use completely different technical routes, but it does not clearly characterize their approaches as fundamentally similar despite implementation differences.

r002.rationale: It says reinforcement learning can use success or failure feedback when a task’s result is verifiable, but does not identify seeking such settings as a shared strategy of both companies.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that experience showed each company’s reinforcement-learning implementation could work.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions: what signals you train on, and how you organize the process of improving a model. I don’t have visibility into both companies’ internal recipes, so I’d be careful about drawing a sharp line between them.

At a conceptual level, post-training turns a model’s broad capabilities into useful behavior. Reinforcement learning is one way to do that, but the key question is: what are you rewarding? Human preference, following a set of principles, getting a verifiable answer right, or successfully completing a task can produce quite different behaviors.

The distinction people often draw is that OpenAI emphasizes reinforcement learning as a way to improve capability, while Anthropic emphasizes principles and alignment in shaping behavior. That’s a useful framing, but it can become misleading if you treat it as an exclusive choice. You need both capability and a way to specify which behavior you actually want.

For agents, I think the more interesting comparison is how each approach handles a long sequence of actions. Getting a single response rated highly is different from completing a task over many steps. Can the model explore, recognize a mistake, recover, and ultimately achieve the user’s goal? Then the quality of the environment, the feedback, and the evaluation becomes at least as important as the particular reinforcement learning algorithm.

r001.rationale: The response says capability and behavioral alignment are both needed, but does not characterize the companies’ approaches as fundamentally similar despite implementation differences.

r002.rationale: It mentions verifiable answers as one possible reward signal, but does not identify clear, objective feedback settings as a strategy shared by both companies.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that experience showed both companies’ reinforcement-learning implementations could work.
